Variants.Content: The Bigods held the hereditary office of Earl Marshal of England from Framlingham in Suffolk, a castle whose thirteen towers overlooked the East Anglian meres. Roger Bigod, 5th Earl of Norfolk, openly defied Henry III's threats in Westminster Hall in 1258 and joined the barons who pressed the Provisions of Oxford on the crown. His brother Hugh Bigod served as Chief Justiciar and worked to clean up shire administration, which had grown corrupt under royal favorites. The Earl Marshal supervised the military order and ceremony of the realm, so the family's authority ran through the army as well as the courts. Their prestige made the reform programme look legitimate to the county knights.

Directing army muster rolls and knightly codes, the Earl Marshal's authority was essential to legitimize the 1258 Provisions of Oxford across the kingdom. Each muster summons carried his name, so a lord who ignored the call risked a fine and a loss of standing at court.

Framlingham's walls make the earl's power visible to the surrounding countryside. A tenant approaching his court still worries about rent, fines and the cost of a dispute. Protection against a stranger's demands can matter, but it is no proof that every officer is fair. A poor petitioner needs witnesses and a recognised claim, rather than confidence in the family's reputation alone.
